questions.q: A particle moves from an initial point $A(1, 2, -1)$ m to a final point $B(x, 4, 2)$ m under the influence of a constant force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$ N. If the total work done by the force is $14$ J, the value of the coordinate $x$ is:
questions.question: A particle moves from an initial point $A(1, 2, -1)$ m to a final point $B(x, 4, 2)$ m under the influence of a constant force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$ N. If the total work done by the force is $14$ J, the value of the coordinate $x$ is:
questions.solution:
The displacement vector $\vec{s}$ of the particle is given by the difference between the final and initial position vectors:
$\vec{s} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$
$\vec{s} = (x - 1)\hat{i} + (4 - 2)\hat{j} + (2 - (-1))\hat{k}$
$\vec{s} = (x - 1)\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ m

The work done $W$ by a constant force is the dot product of the force and displacement vectors:
$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}$
$W = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}) \cdot ((x - 1)\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})$
$W = 3(x - 1) + (-2)(2) + (4)(3)$
$W = 3x - 3 - 4 + 12$
$W = 3x + 5$

Given that the total work done is $14$ J:
$3x + 5 = 14$
$3x = 9$
$x = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $L$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. At its lowest point, the pendulum bob collides with a rigid vertical wall. After rebounding, the pendulum swings back up to a maximum angle $\theta$ with the vertical, such that $\cos\theta = 0.64$. The percentage loss of mechanical energy during the collision and the coefficient of restitution between the bob and the wall, respectively, are :
questions.question: A simple pendulum of length $L$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. At its lowest point, the pendulum bob collides with a rigid vertical wall. After rebounding, the pendulum swings back up to a maximum angle $\theta$ with the vertical, such that $\cos\theta = 0.64$. The percentage loss of mechanical energy during the collision and the coefficient of restitution between the bob and the wall, respectively, are :
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the pendulum bob be $m$.

The initial mechanical energy of the bob relative to the lowest point is:
$E_i = mgL$

After the collision, the bob rebounds and reaches a maximum angle $\theta$ with the vertical. The maximum height reached by the bob is:
$h = L(1 - \cos\theta) = L(1 - 0.64) = 0.36L$

The mechanical energy of the bob just after the collision is:
$E_f = mgh = 0.36mgL$

The loss in mechanical energy during the collision is:
$\Delta E = E_i - E_f = mgL - 0.36mgL = 0.64mgL$

The percentage loss of mechanical energy is:
$\%\text{ loss} = \left(\dfrac{\Delta E}{E_i}\right) \times 100 = \left(\dfrac{0.64mgL}{mgL}\right) \times 100 = 64\%$

The coefficient of restitution $e$ is the ratio of the speed just after collision to the speed just before collision:
$e = \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{\dfrac{E_f}{E_i}} = \sqrt{0.36} = 0.6$

Thus, the percentage loss of energy is $64\%$ and the coefficient of restitution is $0.6$.

Answer: $64\%, 0.6$

questions.q: A small block is released from rest from the top of a smooth curved track. The track ends at the ground level. When the block is at a vertical height of $2\text{ m}$ above the ground, its speed is $4\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. If $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the vertical height from which the block was released is:
questions.question: A small block is released from rest from the top of a smooth curved track. The track ends at the ground level. When the block is at a vertical height of $2\text{ m}$ above the ground, its speed is $4\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. If $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the vertical height from which the block was released is:
questions.solution:
Let the initial height of the block be $H$.

Applying conservation of mechanical energy between the release point and the point at height $h = 2\text{ m}$:

$m g H = m g h + \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

Substituting the given values ($g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $h = 2\text{ m}$, $v = 4\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$):

$10 \times H = 10 \times 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times (4\sqrt{5})^2$

$10 H = 20 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 80$

$10 H = 20 + 40 = 60$

$H = 6\text{ m}$

Answer: $6\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $L$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. During its downward swing, at a certain angle $\theta$ from the vertical, the net acceleration vector of the bob becomes purely horizontal. The value of $\theta$ is :
questions.question: A simple pendulum of length $L$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. During its downward swing, at a certain angle $\theta$ from the vertical, the net acceleration vector of the bob becomes purely horizontal. The value of $\theta$ is :
questions.solution:
Let the string make an angle $\theta$ with the vertical.

Since the pendulum is released from the horizontal position, the vertical distance fallen by the bob is $h = L \cos\theta$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity $v$ of the bob is:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgL \cos\theta \Rightarrow v^2 = 2gL \cos\theta$

The centripetal acceleration is directed along the string towards the point of suspension:
$a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{L} = 2g \cos\theta$

The tangential acceleration is directed perpendicular to the string, downwards along the tangent:
$a_t = g \sin\theta$

For the net acceleration vector to be purely horizontal, its vertical component must be zero. We resolve $a_c$ and $a_t$ in the vertical direction.

The upward vertical component of $a_c$ is $a_c \cos\theta$.
The downward vertical component of $a_t$ is $a_t \sin\theta$.

Equating the upward and downward vertical components:
$a_c \cos\theta = a_t \sin\theta$

Substituting the expressions for $a_c$ and $a_t$:
$(2g \cos\theta)\cos\theta = (g \sin\theta)\sin\theta$
$\Rightarrow 2g \cos^2\theta = g \sin^2\theta$
$\Rightarrow \tan^2\theta = 2$
$\Rightarrow \tan\theta = \sqrt{2}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$

Answer: $\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet of mass $10$ g is fired horizontally with a speed of $400$ m/s into a stationary wooden block of mass $390$ g resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The bullet penetrates $20$ cm into the block and comes to rest inside it as the block begins to slide. The average resistive force exerted by the wooden block on the bullet is:
questions.question: A bullet of mass $10$ g is fired horizontally with a speed of $400$ m/s into a stationary wooden block of mass $390$ g resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The bullet penetrates $20$ cm into the block and comes to rest inside it as the block begins to slide. The average resistive force exerted by the wooden block on the bullet is:
questions.solution:
By conservation of linear momentum along the horizontal direction, the common velocity $v$ of the block and bullet after penetration is:

$mu = (m + M)v$

$v = \dfrac{mu}{m + M}$

Given $m = 0.01$ kg, $u = 400$ m/s, and $M = 0.39$ kg:

$v = \dfrac{0.01 \times 400}{0.01 + 0.39} = \dfrac{4}{0.4} = 10$ m/s

The initial kinetic energy of the system is:

$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.01 \times (400)^2 = 800$ J

The final kinetic energy of the system is:

$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}(m + M)v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times (10)^2 = 20$ J

The loss in kinetic energy is equal to the work done by the internal resistive force $F$ over the penetration depth $d$:

$Fd = K_i - K_f$

$F \times 0.2 = 800 - 20 = 780$

$F = \dfrac{780}{0.2} = 3900$ N

Answer: $3900$ N

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is moved from the origin $(0,0)$ to a point $(d, h)$ in a uniform vertical gravitational field acting in the negative $y$-direction. The particle is taken along three distinct paths: Path 1 is a straight line connecting the two points, Path 2 is a parabolic curve, and Path 3 runs along the $x$-axis to $(d,0)$ and then parallel to the $y$-axis to $(d,h)$. If $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_3$ are the work done by gravity on the particle along these three paths respectively, then the ratio $W_1 : W_2 : W_3$ is:
questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is moved from the origin $(0,0)$ to a point $(d, h)$ in a uniform vertical gravitational field acting in the negative $y$-direction. The particle is taken along three distinct paths: Path 1 is a straight line connecting the two points, Path 2 is a parabolic curve, and Path 3 runs along the $x$-axis to $(d,0)$ and then parallel to the $y$-axis to $(d,h)$. If $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_3$ are the work done by gravity on the particle along these three paths respectively, then the ratio $W_1 : W_2 : W_3$ is:
questions.solution:
The gravitational force is a conservative force, which means the work done by it depends only on the initial and final positions of the particle and is independent of the path taken.

The force of gravity acts in the negative $y$-direction, so the work done by gravity is given by $W = -mg(y_f - y_i)$.

For all three paths, the initial $y$-coordinate is $0$ and the final $y$-coordinate is $h$. Therefore, the work done by gravity along each path is $-mgh$.

Thus, $W_1 = W_2 = W_3 = -mgh$, and the ratio $W_1 : W_2 : W_3$ is $1 : 1 : 1$.

Answer: $1 : 1 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block is released from rest from the horizontal rim of a smooth fixed hemispherical bowl of radius $R$. The block slides down the inner surface of the bowl. At a certain position, the net acceleration vector of the block makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with its velocity vector. The angle $\theta$ made by the radius vector of the block with the horizontal at this position is :
questions.question: A small block is released from rest from the horizontal rim of a smooth fixed hemispherical bowl of radius $R$. The block slides down the inner surface of the bowl. At a certain position, the net acceleration vector of the block makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with its velocity vector. The angle $\theta$ made by the radius vector of the block with the horizontal at this position is :
questions.solution:
Let the radius vector of the block make an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal.

The vertical distance descended by the block is $h = R \sin\theta$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity $v$ of the block is given by:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgR \sin\theta \Rightarrow v^2 = 2gR \sin\theta$

The centripetal acceleration of the block is:
$a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = 2g \sin\theta$

The tangential acceleration of the block is the component of acceleration due to gravity along the tangent:
$a_t = g \cos\theta$

Since the velocity vector is directed along the tangent, the angle $\alpha$ between the net acceleration vector and the velocity vector satisfies:
$\tan\alpha = \dfrac{a_c}{a_t}$

Given that $\alpha = 45^{\circ}$, we have $\tan 45^{\circ} = 1$, which means $a_c = a_t$.

Equating the two components:
$2g \sin\theta = g \cos\theta$
$\Rightarrow \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

Answer: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum consisting of a bob of mass $m$ attached to a string of length $L$ is held such that the string is horizontal. It is then released from rest. What is the kinetic energy of the bob at the instant the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the downward vertical?
questions.question: A simple pendulum consisting of a bob of mass $m$ attached to a string of length $L$ is held such that the string is horizontal. It is then released from rest. What is the kinetic energy of the bob at the instant the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the downward vertical?
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the pendulum's path be the reference level for potential energy.

When the string is horizontal, the height of the bob above the lowest point is $L$.

When the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the downward vertical, the height of the bob above the lowest point is $L - L \cos\theta$.

The vertical distance the bob has fallen is $L - (L - L \cos\theta) = L \cos\theta$.

According to the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy is equal to the gain in kinetic energy.

Loss in potential energy $= mg(L \cos\theta)$.

Since the bob is released from rest, its initial kinetic energy is zero. Thus, the kinetic energy at this instant is $mgL \cos\theta$.

Answer: $mgL \cos\theta$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spherical shell of mass $3\text{ kg}$ is rolling without slipping on a horizontal surface with a speed of $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$. It collides with a horizontal ideal spring and compresses it. If the maximum compression of the spring before the shell momentarily stops is $0.2\text{ m}$, the spring constant of the spring is ______ $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
questions.question: A spherical shell of mass $3\text{ kg}$ is rolling without slipping on a horizontal surface with a speed of $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$. It collides with a horizontal ideal spring and compresses it. If the maximum compression of the spring before the shell momentarily stops is $0.2\text{ m}$, the spring constant of the spring is ______ $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
By the conservation of mechanical energy, the total initial kinetic energy of the rolling spherical shell is entirely converted into the elastic potential energy of the spring at maximum compression.

The total kinetic energy of a rolling spherical shell (hollow sphere) is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a spherical shell, $I = \dfrac{2}{3}mr^2$. With $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}$, we get:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{3}mv^2 = \dfrac{5}{6}mv^2$

Substituting the given values:
$K = \dfrac{5}{6} \times 3 \times (4)^2 = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 16 = 40\text{ J}$

The elastic potential energy stored in the spring is:
$U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

Equating the energies ($K = U$):
$40 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times k \times (0.2)^2$
$40 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times k \times 0.04$
$40 = 0.02 k$
$k = \dfrac{40}{0.02} = 2000\text{ N m}^{-1}$

Answer: $2000$

$x$ (m)$0$$1$$2$$3$
$v$ (m/s)$2$$4$$6$$8$


The work done by the net force on the particle during the displacement from $x = 1$ m to $x = 3$ m is:
questions.question:
A particle of mass $4$ kg moves along a straight line. The velocity $v$ of the particle at various positions $x$ is recorded in the table below:

$x$ (m)$0$$1$$2$$3$
$v$ (m/s)$2$$4$$6$$8$


The work done by the net force on the particle during the displacement from $x = 1$ m to $x = 3$ m is:
questions.solution:
From the given table, the initial velocity of the particle at $x = 1$ m is $v_i = 4$ m/s.

The final velocity at $x = 3$ m is $v_f = 8$ m/s.

According to the work-energy theorem, the work done by the net force is equal to the change in kinetic energy:

$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} m (v_f^2 - v_i^2)$

Substituting the given values ($m = 4$ kg):

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (8^2 - 4^2)$

$W = 2 \times (64 - 16) = 2 \times 48 = 96$ J.

Answer: $96$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is released from rest on a rough inclined plane that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $\mu$. What is the kinetic energy of the block after it has slid a distance $d$ down the plane?
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is released from rest on a rough inclined plane that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $\mu$. What is the kinetic energy of the block after it has slid a distance $d$ down the plane?
questions.solution:
The forces doing work on the block as it slides down the incline are gravity and kinetic friction.

The component of the gravitational force along the incline is $mg \sin\theta$. The work done by gravity over a distance $d$ is $W_g = mgd \sin\theta$.

The normal force on the block is $N = mg \cos\theta$. The kinetic friction force opposes the motion and has a magnitude $f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos\theta$.

The work done by friction is $W_f = -f_k d = -\mu mgd \cos\theta$.

According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy.

$\Delta K = W_g + W_f$

$K - 0 = mgd \sin\theta - \mu mgd \cos\theta$

$K = mgd(\sin\theta - \mu \cos\theta)$

Answer: $mgd(\sin\theta - \mu \cos\theta)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum bob of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. The length of the pendulum is $2\text{ m}$. When the bob arrives at the lowest point of its path, the tension in the string is measured to be $13\text{ N}$. The percentage of the initial potential energy that was dissipated against air resistance during the fall is: [Use $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question: A pendulum bob of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from a horizontal position. The length of the pendulum is $2\text{ m}$. When the bob arrives at the lowest point of its path, the tension in the string is measured to be $13\text{ N}$. The percentage of the initial potential energy that was dissipated against air resistance during the fall is: [Use $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the bob at the lowest point be $v$.
At the lowest point, the net force towards the center provides the necessary centripetal acceleration:
$T - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{L}$

Substitute the given values ($m = 0.5\text{ kg}$, $L = 2\text{ m}$, $T = 13\text{ N}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$):
$13 - (0.5 \times 10) = \dfrac{0.5 \times v^2}{2}$
$13 - 5 = 0.25 v^2$
$8 = 0.25 v^2$
$v^2 = 32\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$

The final kinetic energy of the bob at the lowest point is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 32 = 8\text{ J}$

The initial potential energy of the bob at the horizontal position (taking the lowest point as the reference level) is:
$U = mgL = 0.5 \times 10 \times 2 = 10\text{ J}$

The energy dissipated against air resistance is the difference between the initial potential energy and the final kinetic energy:
$E_{\text{dissipated}} = U - K = 10\text{ J} - 8\text{ J} = 2\text{ J}$

The percentage of the initial potential energy dissipated is:
$\text{Percentage} = \left( \dfrac{E_{\text{dissipated}}}{U} \right) \times 100\%$
$\text{Percentage} = \left( \dfrac{2}{10} \right) \times 100\% = 20\%$

Answer: $20\%$

questions.q:
A block of mass $20\text{ kg}$ initially at rest on a rough horizontal surface is pulled by a horizontal rope with a constant acceleration of $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.4$, the power delivered by the rope at $t = 4\text{ s}$ from the start is _____ $\text{W}$.
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question:
A block of mass $20\text{ kg}$ initially at rest on a rough horizontal surface is pulled by a horizontal rope with a constant acceleration of $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.4$, the power delivered by the rope at $t = 4\text{ s}$ from the start is _____ $\text{W}$.
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
Let the tension in the rope be $T$.

Using Newton's second law for the block in the horizontal direction:
$T - \mu_k mg = ma$
$T = m(a + \mu_k g)$

Substituting the given values:
$T = 20(2 + 0.4 \times 10)$
$T = 20(2 + 4) = 120\text{ N}$

The velocity of the block at $t = 4\text{ s}$ is:
$v = u + at$
$v = 0 + 2 \times 4 = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$

The power delivered by the rope at $t = 4\text{ s}$ is:
$P = T \times v$
$P = 120 \times 8 = 960\text{ W}$

Answer: $960$

questions.q: A block of mass $2$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal surface by an external force. The velocity of the block varies with its position $x$ as $v = 3x$, where $v$ is in m/s and $x$ is in m. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$, the work done by the external force during the displacement of the block from $x = 0$ m to $x = 2$ m is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$):
questions.question: A block of mass $2$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal surface by an external force. The velocity of the block varies with its position $x$ as $v = 3x$, where $v$ is in m/s and $x$ is in m. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$, the work done by the external force during the displacement of the block from $x = 0$ m to $x = 2$ m is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$):
questions.solution:
The initial velocity of the block at $x = 0$ m is $v_i = 3(0) = 0$ m/s.

The final velocity at $x = 2$ m is $v_f = 3(2) = 6$ m/s.

The change in kinetic energy of the block is:

$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} m (v_f^2 - v_i^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (6^2 - 0) = 36$ J.

The work done by the kinetic friction force is:

$W_{fric} = -\mu_k m g d = -0.5 \times 2 \times 10 \times 2 = -20$ J.

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy:

$W_{ext} + W_{fric} = \Delta K$

$W_{ext} - 20 = 36$

$W_{ext} = 56$ J.

Answer: $56$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is rolling on a horizontal surface. The absolute value of the work required to bring it to a complete stop is $140\text{ J}$. The initial speed of the center of mass of the sphere is ______ $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
questions.question: A solid sphere of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is rolling on a horizontal surface. The absolute value of the work required to bring it to a complete stop is $140\text{ J}$. The initial speed of the center of mass of the sphere is ______ $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the work done to stop the rolling sphere is equal to its initial total kinetic energy.

The total kinetic energy of a rolling solid sphere is the sum of its translational and rotational kinetic energies:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$. Since it is rolling without slipping, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}$.

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{5}mv^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

Equating this to the work done:
$W = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$
$140 = \dfrac{7}{10} \times 2 \times v^2$
$140 = 1.4 v^2$
$v^2 = 100$
$v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is moving in the $xy$-plane such that its velocity vector as a function of time $t$ is given by $\vec{v}(t) = (p t^2)\hat{i} + (q t)\hat{j}$. The work done by all the forces acting on the particle during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$ is (Take $p = 1\text{ m/s}^3$ and $q = 2\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.question: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is moving in the $xy$-plane such that its velocity vector as a function of time $t$ is given by $\vec{v}(t) = (p t^2)\hat{i} + (q t)\hat{j}$. The work done by all the forces acting on the particle during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$ is (Take $p = 1\text{ m/s}^3$ and $q = 2\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the work done by all forces on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.

The velocity vector of the particle is given by:
$\vec{v}(t) = (1 \cdot t^2)\hat{i} + (2 \cdot t)\hat{j} = t^2\hat{i} + 2t\hat{j}$

At $t = 0$, the initial velocity is:
$\vec{v}(0) = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} = \vec{0}$
Initial kinetic energy, $K_i = 0$

At $t = 2\text{ s}$, the final velocity is:
$\vec{v}(2) = (2^2)\hat{i} + (2 \cdot 2)\hat{j} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$

The square of the final speed is:
$|\vec{v}(2)|^2 = 4^2 + 4^2 = 16 + 16 = 32\text{ (m/s)}^2$

Final kinetic energy, $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}m|\vec{v}(2)|^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 32 = 32\text{ J}$

Work done, $W = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = 32 - 0 = 32\text{ J}$

Answer: $32\text{ J}$

The first $2$ m of the incline is perfectly smooth, while the remaining $6$ m is rough. If the block comes to rest exactly at the bottom of the rough section, the coefficient of kinetic friction of the rough section is:

questions.question:
A block is released from rest at the top of an inclined plane making an angle of $37^\circ$ with the horizontal. The first $2$ m of the incline is perfectly smooth, while the remaining $6$ m is rough. If the block comes to rest exactly at the bottom of the rough section, the coefficient of kinetic friction of the rough section is:
(Take $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\cos 37^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.solution:
Using the work-energy theorem, the total work done on the block is equal to its change in kinetic energy.

Since the block starts from rest and finally comes to rest, $\Delta K = 0$.

The forces doing work are gravity (over the entire length $L_1 + L_2$) and kinetic friction (only over the rough section $L_2$).

$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} = 0$

$mg(L_1 + L_2)\sin\theta - \mu_k mg \cos\theta L_2 = 0$

$(L_1 + L_2)\sin\theta = \mu_k L_2 \cos\theta$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{L_1 + L_2}{L_2} \tan\theta$

Given $L_1 = 2$ m, $L_2 = 6$ m, and $\theta = 37^\circ$:

$\mu_k = \dfrac{2 + 6}{6} \times \tan 37^\circ$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{8}{6} \times \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 1.0$

Answer: $1.0$

On this smooth portion, the block collides with an ideal horizontal spring of spring constant $k = 200\text{ N/m}$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, the maximum compression of the spring is
questions.question: A block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is projected with an initial velocity of $6\text{ m/s}$ at $x = 0$ on a horizontal track. The track has a rough patch from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$, where the coefficient of kinetic friction varies with position as $\mu_k = 0.1x$. Beyond $x = 2\text{ m}$, the track is frictionless. On this smooth portion, the block collides with an ideal horizontal spring of spring constant $k = 200\text{ N/m}$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, the maximum compression of the spring is
questions.solution:
The frictional force acting on the block in the rough region is variable and given by:
$f_k = \mu_k mg = (0.1x)(1)(10) = x\text{ N}$

The work done by friction as the block moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$ is:
$W_f = \int_{0}^{2} -f_k dx = \int_{0}^{2} -x dx = -\left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} = -\dfrac{4}{2} = -2\text{ J}$

By the work-energy theorem, the total work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy. When the spring reaches maximum compression $x_m$, the block's final velocity is zero.
$W_f + W_s = K_f - K_i$
$-2 + \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} k x_m^2 \right) = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v_0^2$

Substitute the given values ($m = 1\text{ kg}$, $v_0 = 6\text{ m/s}$, $k = 200\text{ N/m}$):
$-2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(200) x_m^2 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(1)(36)$
$-2 - 100 x_m^2 = -18$
$100 x_m^2 = 16$
$x_m^2 = 0.16\text{ m}^2$
$x_m = 0.4\text{ m} = 40\text{ cm}$

Answer: $40\text{ cm}$

questions.q:
A small stone is tied to a string of length $2 \text{ m}$ and whirled in a vertical circle. At the lowest point, its speed is $\sqrt{7gL}$. When the stone is ascending and the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the upward vertical, the string is suddenly cut. The stone then moves freely under gravity as a projectile. The maximum height reached by the stone from the lowest point of the circular path is :

(Take acceleration due to gravity as $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question:
A small stone is tied to a string of length $2 \text{ m}$ and whirled in a vertical circle. At the lowest point, its speed is $\sqrt{7gL}$. When the stone is ascending and the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the upward vertical, the string is suddenly cut. The stone then moves freely under gravity as a projectile. The maximum height reached by the stone from the lowest point of the circular path is :

(Take acceleration due to gravity as $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the circular path be the reference level ($h = 0$).

The initial speed at the lowest point is $u = \sqrt{7gL}$.

When the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the upward vertical, the angle it makes with the downward vertical is $180^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 120^{\circ}$.
The height of the stone at the instant the string is cut is:
$h_c = L - L\cos(120^{\circ}) = L - L\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3L}{2}$
Substituting $L = 2 \text{ m}$, we get $h_c = 3 \text{ m}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, the speed $v_c$ of the stone at this point is:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_c^2 + mgh_c$
$v_c^2 = u^2 - 2gh_c = 7gL - 2g\left(\dfrac{3L}{2}\right) = 7gL - 3gL = 4gL$
Substituting $L = 2 \text{ m}$ and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:
$v_c^2 = 4 \times 10 \times 2 = 80 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$

At the instant the string is cut, the velocity vector is tangential to the circular path. Since the string (radial vector) makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical, the velocity vector (perpendicular to the string) makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal.
Thus, the stone becomes a projectile with an initial speed $v_c$ and an angle of projection $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$.

The maximum height gained by the stone during its projectile motion, measured from the point of release, is:
$H_{proj} = \dfrac{v_c^2 \sin^2 \alpha}{2g}$
$H_{proj} = \dfrac{80 \times \sin^2(60^{\circ})}{2 \times 10} = \dfrac{80 \times \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2}{20} = 4 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 3 \text{ m}$

The total maximum height reached by the stone from the lowest point of the circular path is:
$H_{total} = h_c + H_{proj} = 3 \text{ m} + 3 \text{ m} = 6 \text{ m}$

Answer: $6 \text{ m}$

A small bead slides on a smooth vertical circular wire of radius $25\text{ m}$. It is released from rest at a point $A$ on the wire and reaches the lowest point $B$ with a speed of $10\text{ m/s}$. The angle $\theta$ that the radius vector to point $A$ makes with the downward vertical is:

(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question:
A small bead slides on a smooth vertical circular wire of radius $25\text{ m}$. It is released from rest at a point $A$ on the wire and reaches the lowest point $B$ with a speed of $10\text{ m/s}$. The angle $\theta$ that the radius vector to point $A$ makes with the downward vertical is:

(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the vertical height dropped by the bead from point $A$ to the lowest point $B$ be $h$.

Applying the Work-Energy Theorem (or conservation of mechanical energy) between $A$ and $B$:
$\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = mgh$
$v^2 = 2gh$

Substituting the given values ($v = 10\text{ m/s}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
$(10)^2 = 2(10)h$
$100 = 20h \Rightarrow h = 5\text{ m}$

From the geometry of the vertical circle, the height $h$ is related to the angle $\theta$ with the downward vertical by:
$h = R(1 - \cos\theta)$

Substituting $R = 25\text{ m}$ and $h = 5\text{ m}$:
$5 = 25(1 - \cos\theta)$
$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{25} = 0.2$
$\cos\theta = 0.8 = \dfrac{4}{5}$

Therefore, $\theta = 37^\circ$.

Answer: $37^\circ$

The work done on the body during the time interval from $t = 1$ s to $t = 2$ s is
questions.question: A body of mass $2$ kg is moving in the $xy$-plane such that its position vector as a function of time is given by $\vec{r}(t) = 2t^2\hat{i} + t^3\hat{j}$ (where $\vec{r}$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds). The work done on the body during the time interval from $t = 1$ s to $t = 2$ s is
questions.solution:
The velocity vector is the time derivative of the position vector:
$\vec{v}(t) = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = 4t\hat{i} + 3t^2\hat{j}$

At $t = 1$ s, the initial velocity vector is:
$\vec{v}_1 = 4(1)\hat{i} + 3(1)^2\hat{j} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$ m/s
The square of its magnitude is:
$v_1^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 9 = 25$ m$^2$/s$^2$

At $t = 2$ s, the final velocity vector is:
$\vec{v}_2 = 4(2)\hat{i} + 3(2)^2\hat{j} = 8\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$ m/s
The square of its magnitude is:
$v_2^2 = 8^2 + 12^2 = 64 + 144 = 208$ m$^2$/s$^2$

Using the work-energy theorem, the total work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta KE = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(208 - 25) = 183$ J

Answer: $183$ J

questions.q: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moves in the horizontal $x-y$ plane under the influence of a net force $\vec{F} = (kx \hat{i} + 4y \hat{j})\text{ N}$, where $k$ is a constant. The particle moves from the initial position $(0, 1)\text{ m}$ to the final position $(2, 2)\text{ m}$, and its speed increases from $2\text{ m/s}$ to $4\text{ m/s}$. The value of the constant $k$ is :
questions.question: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moves in the horizontal $x-y$ plane under the influence of a net force $\vec{F} = (kx \hat{i} + 4y \hat{j})\text{ N}$, where $k$ is a constant. The particle moves from the initial position $(0, 1)\text{ m}$ to the final position $(2, 2)\text{ m}$, and its speed increases from $2\text{ m/s}$ to $4\text{ m/s}$. The value of the constant $k$ is :
questions.solution:
Using the Work-Energy Theorem, the net work done on the particle equals its change in kinetic energy.

The change in kinetic energy is:
$\Delta KE = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$
$\Delta KE = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(4^2 - 2^2) = 16 - 4 = 12\text{ J}$

The work done by the variable force is the line integral from $(0, 1)$ to $(2, 2)$:
$W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{0}^{2} kx \, dx + \int_{1}^{2} 4y \, dy$
$W = \left[ \dfrac{kx^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} + \left[ \dfrac{4y^2}{2} \right]_{1}^{2}$
$W = \dfrac{k}{2}(4 - 0) + 2(4 - 1)$
$W = 2k + 6$

Equating the work done to the change in kinetic energy:
$2k + 6 = 12$
$2k = 6$
$k = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.q:
A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ starting from rest is pulled up a smooth inclined plane making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal by a constant force parallel to the incline. If the power delivered by the pulling force at $t = 4\text{ s}$ from the start is $560\text{ W}$, the distance covered by the block in the first $4\text{ s}$ is _____ $\text{m}$.
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question:
A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ starting from rest is pulled up a smooth inclined plane making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal by a constant force parallel to the incline. If the power delivered by the pulling force at $t = 4\text{ s}$ from the start is $560\text{ W}$, the distance covered by the block in the first $4\text{ s}$ is _____ $\text{m}$.
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
Let the constant acceleration of the block be $a$ and the pulling force be $F$.

Using Newton's second law along the incline:
$F - mg \sin 30^\circ = ma$
$F = 10(a + 10 \times 0.5) = 10(a + 5)$

The velocity of the block at $t = 4\text{ s}$ is:
$v = u + at = 0 + a(4) = 4a$

The power delivered by the pulling force at $t = 4\text{ s}$ is given by:
$P = F \times v$
$560 = 10(a + 5) \times 4a$
$560 = 40a(a + 5)$
$a^2 + 5a - 14 = 0$
$(a + 7)(a - 2) = 0$

Since acceleration must be positive in the direction of motion, $a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

The distance covered by the block in the first $4\text{ s}$ is:
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4)^2 = 16\text{ m}$

Answer: $16$

questions.q:
A small sphere of mass $m$ is attached to a string of length $1 \text{ m}$ to form a simple pendulum. It is given a horizontal velocity $v$ at the lowest position. The ratio of its kinetic energy when the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the downward vertical to its kinetic energy when the string is horizontal is exactly $3:1$. The initial velocity $v$ at the lowest point is :

(Take acceleration due to gravity as $10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question:
A small sphere of mass $m$ is attached to a string of length $1 \text{ m}$ to form a simple pendulum. It is given a horizontal velocity $v$ at the lowest position. The ratio of its kinetic energy when the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the downward vertical to its kinetic energy when the string is horizontal is exactly $3:1$. The initial velocity $v$ at the lowest point is :

(Take acceleration due to gravity as $10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point be the reference level for potential energy ($h = 0$).

The initial kinetic energy at the lowest point is:
$K_0 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

When the string makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the downward vertical, the vertical height of the sphere is:
$h_1 = L - L\cos(60^{\circ}) = 1 - 1 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5 \text{ m}$

By conservation of mechanical energy, the kinetic energy at this position is:
$K_1 = K_0 - mgh_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - m(10)(0.5) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 5m$

When the string is horizontal, the angle with the downward vertical is $90^{\circ}$, and the vertical height is:
$h_2 = L = 1 \text{ m}$

The kinetic energy at this horizontal position is:
$K_2 = K_0 - mgh_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - m(10)(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 10m$

We are given that the ratio of these kinetic energies is $3:1$:
$\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = 3$
$\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 5m}{\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 10m} = 3$

Cancelling $m$ and cross-multiplying:
$\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 - 5 = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 - 10\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 - 5 = \dfrac{3}{2}v^2 - 30$

Rearranging the terms:
$\dfrac{3}{2}v^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = 30 - 5$
$v^2 = 25$
$v = 5 \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $5 \text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A block of mass $20\text{ kg}$ is pushed along a horizontal floor for a distance of $5\text{ m}$. If the total work done against friction during this displacement is $250\text{ J}$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is: (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question: A block of mass $20\text{ kg}$ is pushed along a horizontal floor for a distance of $5\text{ m}$. If the total work done against friction during this displacement is $250\text{ J}$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is: (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Given:
Mass of the block, $m = 20\text{ kg}$
Distance moved, $d = 5\text{ m}$
Work done against friction, $W = 250\text{ J}$

The work done against friction is given by the formula:
$W = f_k d = \mu_k m g d$

Rearranging for the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$:
$\mu_k = \dfrac{W}{m g d}$

Substituting the given values:
$\mu_k = \dfrac{250}{20 \times 10 \times 5}$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{250}{1000} = 0.25$

Answer: $0.25$

questions.q: A bullet of mass $0.1\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally with a speed of $100\text{ m s}^{-1}$ strikes and embeds itself into a block of mass $1.9\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal surface. The block is attached to one end of a relaxed horizontal spring of spring constant $160\text{ N m}^{-1}$, the other end of which is fixed to a vertical wall. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$. The maximum compression of the spring before the combined mass comes to rest is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A bullet of mass $0.1\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally with a speed of $100\text{ m s}^{-1}$ strikes and embeds itself into a block of mass $1.9\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal surface. The block is attached to one end of a relaxed horizontal spring of spring constant $160\text{ N m}^{-1}$, the other end of which is fixed to a vertical wall. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$. The maximum compression of the spring before the combined mass comes to rest is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
By conservation of linear momentum during the perfectly inelastic collision:
$m u = (m + M) v$
$0.1 \times 100 = (0.1 + 1.9) v$
$10 = 2 v \Rightarrow v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Initial kinetic energy of the combined mass just after the collision:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}(m + M)v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(5)^2 = 25\text{ J}$

Let the maximum compression of the spring be $x$. By the work-energy theorem, the initial kinetic energy is dissipated by friction and stored as elastic potential energy in the spring:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + \mu(m + M)gx$
$25 = \dfrac{1}{2}(160)x^2 + 0.5(2)(10)x$
$25 = 80x^2 + 10x$

Dividing by 5 and rearranging yields a quadratic equation:
$16x^2 + 2x - 5 = 0$

Solving for $x$ using the quadratic formula:
$x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{2^2 - 4(16)(-5)}}{2(16)}$
$x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 320}}{32} = \dfrac{-2 \pm 18}{32}$

Taking the physically meaningful positive root:
$x = \dfrac{16}{32} = 0.50\text{ m}$

Answer: $0.50\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is initially at rest at the origin. It is acted upon by a time-dependent force given by $\vec{F} = F_{0} \cos(\omega t) \hat{i} + F_{0} \sin(\omega t) \hat{j}$. The power developed by this force as a function of time $t$ is:
questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is initially at rest at the origin. It is acted upon by a time-dependent force given by $\vec{F} = F_{0} \cos(\omega t) \hat{i} + F_{0} \sin(\omega t) \hat{j}$. The power developed by this force as a function of time $t$ is:
questions.solution:
Given force $\vec{F} = F_{0} \cos(\omega t) \hat{i} + F_{0} \sin(\omega t) \hat{j}$.

The acceleration of the particle is:
$\vec{a} = \dfrac{\vec{F}}{m} = \dfrac{F_{0}}{m} \cos(\omega t) \hat{i} + \dfrac{F_{0}}{m} \sin(\omega t) \hat{j}$

Since the particle starts from rest, its velocity $\vec{v}$ at time $t$ is obtained by integrating the acceleration:
$\vec{v} = \int_{0}^{t} \vec{a} dt$
$\vec{v} = \int_{0}^{t} \left( \dfrac{F_{0}}{m} \cos(\omega t) \hat{i} + \dfrac{F_{0}}{m} \sin(\omega t) \hat{j} \right) dt$
$\vec{v} = \left[ \dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} \sin(\omega t) \right]_{0}^{t} \hat{i} + \left[ -\dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} \cos(\omega t) \right]_{0}^{t} \hat{j}$
$\vec{v} = \dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} \sin(\omega t) \hat{i} + \dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} (1 - \cos(\omega t)) \hat{j}$

The power developed by the force is the dot product of force and velocity:
$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$
$P = \left( F_{0} \cos(\omega t) \right) \left( \dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} \sin(\omega t) \right) + \left( F_{0} \sin(\omega t) \right) \left( \dfrac{F_{0}}{m\omega} (1 - \cos(\omega t)) \right)$
$P = \dfrac{F_{0}^{2}}{m\omega} \left[ \cos(\omega t) \sin(\omega t) + \sin(\omega t) - \sin(\omega t) \cos(\omega t) \right]$
$P = \dfrac{F_{0}^{2}}{m\omega} \sin(\omega t)$

Answer: $\dfrac{F_{0}^{2}}{m\omega}\sin(\omega t)$

questions.q: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moving along the positive x-axis has an initial velocity of $6\text{ m/s}$ at $x = 0$. It is subjected to a position-dependent force $F$. The force $F$ varies with position $x$ such that the $F-x$ graph forms a triangle: the force is zero at $x = 0$, reaches a minimum value of $-10\text{ N}$ at $x = 2\text{ m}$, and returns to zero at $x = 4\text{ m}$. The velocity of the particle at $x = 4\text{ m}$ is
questions.question: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moving along the positive x-axis has an initial velocity of $6\text{ m/s}$ at $x = 0$. It is subjected to a position-dependent force $F$. The force $F$ varies with position $x$ such that the $F-x$ graph forms a triangle: the force is zero at $x = 0$, reaches a minimum value of $-10\text{ N}$ at $x = 2\text{ m}$, and returns to zero at $x = 4\text{ m}$. The velocity of the particle at $x = 4\text{ m}$ is
questions.solution:
The work done by the variable force is given by the area under the $F-x$ graph.

Since the graph is a triangle with base from $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$ and a peak of $-10\text{ N}$, the area is:
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (-10) = -20\text{ J}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:
$W = K_f - K_i$
$-20 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_f^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v_i^2$

Given $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and $v_i = 6\text{ m/s}$:
$-20 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2) v_f^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(2) (6)^2$
$-20 = v_f^2 - 36$
$v_f^2 = 16$
$v_f = 4\text{ m/s}$

Answer: $4\text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A body of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis such that its position varies with time $t$ according to the equation $x(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + 3t$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. The net work done by the force acting on the body during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\ \text{s}$ is
questions.question: A body of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis such that its position varies with time $t$ according to the equation $x(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + 3t$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. The net work done by the force acting on the body during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\ \text{s}$ is
questions.solution:
The position of the body is given by $x(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + 3t$.

The velocity of the body as a function of time is the derivative of position with respect to time:
$v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 4t + 3$

The initial velocity at $t = 0$ is:
$v(0) = 3(0)^2 - 4(0) + 3 = 3\ \text{m/s}$

The final velocity at $t = 2\ \text{s}$ is:
$v(2) = 3(2)^2 - 4(2) + 3 = 12 - 8 + 3 = 7\ \text{m/s}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$

Substituting the values:
$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(7^2 - 3^2)$
$W = 49 - 9 = 40\ \text{J}$

Answer: $40\ \text{J}$

questions.q:
A simple pendulum of length $2.5\text{ m}$ is displaced such that its string makes an angle of $37^\circ$ with the downward vertical. From this position, the pendulum bob is given an initial speed of $\sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along its circular path towards the lowest point. The speed of the bob when it reaches the lowest point of its path is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$)
questions.question:
A simple pendulum of length $2.5\text{ m}$ is displaced such that its string makes an angle of $37^\circ$ with the downward vertical. From this position, the pendulum bob is given an initial speed of $\sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along its circular path towards the lowest point. The speed of the bob when it reaches the lowest point of its path is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$)
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point be the reference level for potential energy ($U = 0$).

The initial vertical height $h$ of the bob above the lowest point is:
$h = L(1 - \cos 37^\circ)$
$h = 2.5 \times (1 - 0.8) = 2.5 \times 0.2 = 0.5\text{ m}$

Applying conservation of mechanical energy between the initial position and the lowest point:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 + m g h = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

$\Rightarrow v^2 = u^2 + 2 g h$

Substituting the given values ($u = \sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $h = 0.5\text{ m}$):

$v^2 = (\sqrt{6})^2 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.5$

$v^2 = 6 + 10 = 16$

$v = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is pushed slowly up a smooth vertical quarter-circular track of radius $R$, from its lowest point to the horizontal level of its center. The pushing force applied on the block is strictly horizontal at all times. The total work done by this horizontal external force is:
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is pushed slowly up a smooth vertical quarter-circular track of radius $R$, from its lowest point to the horizontal level of its center. The pushing force applied on the block is strictly horizontal at all times. The total work done by this horizontal external force is:
questions.solution:
Since the block is pushed slowly, its kinetic energy remains constant, so the change in kinetic energy is zero ($\Delta K = 0$).

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done by all forces acting on the block is zero:
$W_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{ext}} + W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{normal}} = \Delta K = 0$

The normal force is always perpendicular to the displacement of the block, so the work done by the normal force is $W_{\text{normal}} = 0$.

The work done by gravity as the block moves up by a vertical height $R$ is $W_{\text{gravity}} = -mgR$.

Substituting these into the work-energy equation yields:
$W_{\text{ext}} - mgR + 0 = 0 \Rightarrow W_{\text{ext}} = mgR$.

Answer: $mgR$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small particle attached to a string of length $L$ is given just enough velocity at its lowest point to complete a vertical circle. The magnitude of the change in its velocity as it moves from the position where the string is horizontal to the highest point of the circle is $\sqrt{x gL}$. The value of $x$ is
questions.question: A small particle attached to a string of length $L$ is given just enough velocity at its lowest point to complete a vertical circle. The magnitude of the change in its velocity as it moves from the position where the string is horizontal to the highest point of the circle is $\sqrt{x gL}$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
For a particle to just complete a vertical circle, the tension at the highest point must be zero. This gives the critical velocity at the highest point as $v_{top} = \sqrt{gL}$.

Applying conservation of mechanical energy between the highest point and the horizontal position:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{horiz}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{top}^2 + mgL$
$\Rightarrow v_{horiz}^2 = gL + 2gL = 3gL$
So, the speed at the horizontal position is $v_{horiz} = \sqrt{3gL}$.

The velocity vector at the horizontal position is directed vertically (say, $\hat{j}$), and at the highest point, it is directed horizontally (say, $-\hat{i}$).
$\vec{v}_{horiz} = \sqrt{3gL} \hat{j}$
$\vec{v}_{top} = -\sqrt{gL} \hat{i}$

The change in velocity is $\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}_{top} - \vec{v}_{horiz} = -\sqrt{gL} \hat{i} - \sqrt{3gL} \hat{j}$.
The magnitude of this change is:
$|\Delta \vec{v}| = \sqrt{(\sqrt{gL})^2 + (\sqrt{3gL})^2} = \sqrt{gL + 3gL} = \sqrt{4gL}$

Comparing this with $\sqrt{x gL}$, we get $x = 4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $2\text{ kg}$ starts from rest and moves in a straight line. The power delivered by the net force acting on the body is given as a function of time by $P(t) = 4t^{3}\text{ W}$. The magnitude of the net force acting on the body as a function of time $t$ is:
questions.question: A body of mass $2\text{ kg}$ starts from rest and moves in a straight line. The power delivered by the net force acting on the body is given as a function of time by $P(t) = 4t^{3}\text{ W}$. The magnitude of the net force acting on the body as a function of time $t$ is:
questions.solution:
Given power $P = 4t^{3}\text{ W}$ and mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$.

We know that power is the product of force and velocity:
$P = Fv = (ma)v = m v \dfrac{dv}{dt}$

Substituting the given values:
$4t^{3} = (2) v \dfrac{dv}{dt}$
$2t^{3} dt = v dv$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ to $t$ (since the body starts from rest, $v = 0$ at $t = 0$):
$\int_{0}^{t} 2t^{3} dt = \int_{0}^{v} v dv$
$\dfrac{2t^{4}}{4} = \dfrac{v^{2}}{2}$
$\dfrac{t^{4}}{2} = \dfrac{v^{2}}{2} \Rightarrow v^{2} = t^{4}$

Since the body starts from rest and moves in the direction of the force, $v = t^{2}$.

Now, the acceleration is:
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(t^{2}) = 2t$

The magnitude of the net force is:
$F = ma = 2(2t) = 4t\text{ N}$

Answer: $4t\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is compressed against a horizontal spring of spring constant $400\text{ N m}^{-1}$ by a distance of $0.5\text{ m}$ on a rough horizontal surface. Upon release, the block moves towards the natural length of the spring. If $36\%$ of the initial elastic potential energy is dissipated against friction, the speed of the block when the spring reaches its natural length is:
questions.question: A block of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is compressed against a horizontal spring of spring constant $400\text{ N m}^{-1}$ by a distance of $0.5\text{ m}$ on a rough horizontal surface. Upon release, the block moves towards the natural length of the spring. If $36\%$ of the initial elastic potential energy is dissipated against friction, the speed of the block when the spring reaches its natural length is:
questions.solution:
The initial elastic potential energy stored in the spring is given by:
$U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$
$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 400 \times (0.5)^2 = 50\text{ J}$

It is given that $36\%$ of this initial energy is dissipated against friction. Therefore, the remaining mechanical energy, which converts entirely into the kinetic energy of the block at the natural length, is $100\% - 36\% = 64\%$ of the initial energy.

Final kinetic energy $K = 0.64 \times 50\text{ J} = 32\text{ J}$

Equating this to the kinetic energy formula:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 32$
$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times v^2 = 32$
$0.25 v^2 = 32$
$v^2 = 128$
$v = \sqrt{128} = 8\sqrt{2}\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $8\sqrt{2}\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is whirled in a vertical circle with the help of a string of length $L$. The ratio of the tension in the string at the lowest point to the tension when the string is horizontal is $3$. The magnitude of the change in velocity of the particle as it moves from the lowest point to the horizontal position is $\sqrt{x gL}$. The value of $x$ is
questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is whirled in a vertical circle with the help of a string of length $L$. The ratio of the tension in the string at the lowest point to the tension when the string is horizontal is $3$. The magnitude of the change in velocity of the particle as it moves from the lowest point to the horizontal position is $\sqrt{x gL}$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Let $u$ be the speed at the lowest point and $v$ be the speed at the horizontal position.
The tension at the lowest point is $T_L = \dfrac{mu^2}{L} + mg$.
The tension at the horizontal position is $T_H = \dfrac{mv^2}{L}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy between the lowest and horizontal points:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgL \Rightarrow v^2 = u^2 - 2gL$

Substituting $v^2$ into the expression for $T_H$:
$T_H = \dfrac{m(u^2 - 2gL)}{L} = \dfrac{mu^2}{L} - 2mg$

We are given that $T_L = 3T_H$ :
$\dfrac{mu^2}{L} + mg = 3\left(\dfrac{mu^2}{L} - 2mg\right)$
$\dfrac{mu^2}{L} + mg = \dfrac{3mu^2}{L} - 6mg$
$\Rightarrow 7mg = \dfrac{2mu^2}{L} \Rightarrow u^2 = 3.5gL$

The square of the speed at the horizontal position is:
$v^2 = 3.5gL - 2gL = 1.5gL$

Since the velocity vector at the lowest point is horizontal and at the horizontal position is vertical, they are perpendicular to each other. The magnitude of the change in velocity is:
$|\Delta \vec{v}| = \sqrt{u^2 + v^2} = \sqrt{3.5gL + 1.5gL} = \sqrt{5gL}$

Comparing this with $\sqrt{x gL}$, we get $x = 5$.

Answer: $5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is attached to a relaxed ideal spring of force constant $30\text{ N/m}$. A variable horizontal force $F = F_0 - \alpha x$ (where $x$ is the extension of the spring) is applied to the block in the direction of the extension. If $F_0 = 20\text{ N}$ and $\alpha = 10\text{ N/m}$, the maximum kinetic energy acquired by the block is:
questions.question: A block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is attached to a relaxed ideal spring of force constant $30\text{ N/m}$. A variable horizontal force $F = F_0 - \alpha x$ (where $x$ is the extension of the spring) is applied to the block in the direction of the extension. If $F_0 = 20\text{ N}$ and $\alpha = 10\text{ N/m}$, the maximum kinetic energy acquired by the block is:
questions.solution:
The block acquires maximum kinetic energy when its speed is maximum. This occurs when the net force acting on the block becomes zero.

The forces acting on the block in the horizontal direction are the applied force $F$ and the spring force $F_s = kx$ acting in the opposite direction.

Net force, $F_{\text{net}} = F - F_s = (F_0 - \alpha x) - kx$

For maximum kinetic energy, $F_{\text{net}} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 20 - 10x - 30x = 0$
$\Rightarrow 40x = 20$
$\Rightarrow x = 0.5\text{ m}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the change in kinetic energy is equal to the work done by the net force. Since the block starts from rest, the maximum kinetic energy is the work done by the net force from $x = 0$ to $x = 0.5\text{ m}$.

$W_{\text{net}} = \int_{0}^{0.5} F_{\text{net}} \, dx = \int_{0}^{0.5} (20 - 40x) \, dx$

$W_{\text{net}} = \left[ 20x - \dfrac{40x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{0.5} = \left[ 20x - 20x^2 \right]_{0}^{0.5}$

$W_{\text{net}} = 20(0.5) - 20(0.5)^2 = 10 - 20(0.25) = 10 - 5 = 5\text{ J}$

Thus, the maximum kinetic energy acquired by the block is $5\text{ J}$.

Answer: $5\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from a height of $0.15\text{ m}$ directly above an uncompressed vertical spring fixed to the ground. The spring has a spring constant of $200\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The maximum compression of the spring is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from a height of $0.15\text{ m}$ directly above an uncompressed vertical spring fixed to the ground. The spring has a spring constant of $200\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The maximum compression of the spring is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the maximum compression of the spring be $x$.

Applying the principle of conservation of mechanical energy from the point of release to the point of maximum compression:

Loss in gravitational potential energy = Gain in elastic potential energy

$mg(h + x) = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$

Substituting the given values:

$2 \times 10 \times (0.15 + x) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times x^{2}$

$20(0.15 + x) = 100x^{2}$

$3 + 20x = 100x^{2}$

$100x^{2} - 20x - 3 = 0$

This is a quadratic equation in $x$. Solving for $x$:

$100x^{2} - 30x + 10x - 3 = 0$

$10x(10x - 3) + 1(10x - 3) = 0$

$(10x + 1)(10x - 3) = 0$

Since compression $x$ must be positive, $10x - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0.3\text{ m}$.

Answer: $0.3\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bead of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is threaded on a smooth rigid wire shaped as a parabola $y = x^2$ in the horizontal $x-y$ plane. It is pulled by a non-conservative force $\vec{F} = (3y \hat{i} + 6x \hat{j})\text{ N}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. If the bead starts from rest at the origin $(0,0)$, its kinetic energy when it reaches the position $(2,4)\text{ m}$ is :
questions.question: A bead of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is threaded on a smooth rigid wire shaped as a parabola $y = x^2$ in the horizontal $x-y$ plane. It is pulled by a non-conservative force $\vec{F} = (3y \hat{i} + 6x \hat{j})\text{ N}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. If the bead starts from rest at the origin $(0,0)$, its kinetic energy when it reaches the position $(2,4)\text{ m}$ is :
questions.solution:
The normal force from the smooth wire is perpendicular to the displacement and does zero work. By the Work-Energy Theorem, the kinetic energy of the bead equals the work done by the applied force.

The work done is given by the line integral:
$W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int (3y \, dx + 6x \, dy)$

The bead is constrained to move along the path $y = x^2$. Differentiating this gives $dy = 2x \, dx$.

Substituting $y$ and $dy$ into the integral to express everything in terms of $x$:
$W = \int_{0}^{2} \left( 3(x^2) \, dx + 6x(2x \, dx) \right)$
$W = \int_{0}^{2} (3x^2 + 12x^2) \, dx$
$W = \int_{0}^{2} 15x^2 \, dx$

Evaluating the definite integral:
$W = \left[ \dfrac{15x^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{2} = \left[ 5x^3 \right]_{0}^{2}$
$W = 5(2^3 - 0) = 5(8) = 40\text{ J}$

Since the bead starts from rest, its final kinetic energy is equal to the work done, which is $40\text{ J}$.

Answer: $40\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $2$ kg moves along the $x$-axis such that its displacement as a function of time is given by $x(t) = \alpha t^3 + 18t$ (where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds). If the total work done on the body during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s is $576$ J, the positive value of the constant $\alpha$ is
questions.question: A body of mass $2$ kg moves along the $x$-axis such that its displacement as a function of time is given by $x(t) = \alpha t^3 + 18t$ (where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds). If the total work done on the body during the time interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s is $576$ J, the positive value of the constant $\alpha$ is
questions.solution:
The velocity of the body is given by the derivative of displacement with respect to time:
$v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3\alpha t^2 + 18$

At $t = 0$ s, the initial velocity is:
$v_i = 3\alpha(0)^2 + 18 = 18$ m/s

At $t = 2$ s, the final velocity is:
$v_f = 3\alpha(2)^2 + 18 = 12\alpha + 18$ m/s

According to the work-energy theorem, the work done on the body is equal to its change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta KE = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$

Substitute the given values into the equation:
$576 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)[(12\alpha + 18)^2 - 18^2]$
$576 = (12\alpha + 18)^2 - 324$
$(12\alpha + 18)^2 = 576 + 324 = 900$

Taking the positive square root (since $\alpha$ is positive):
$12\alpha + 18 = 30$
$12\alpha = 12$
$\alpha = 1$

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical blocks, each of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$, are connected by a light spring of spring constant $100\text{ N m}^{-1}$ and placed on a smooth horizontal surface. The spring is initially compressed by $0.1\text{ m}$ and the system is held at rest. If the system is then released, the maximum speed acquired by each block is
questions.question: Two identical blocks, each of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$, are connected by a light spring of spring constant $100\text{ N m}^{-1}$ and placed on a smooth horizontal surface. The spring is initially compressed by $0.1\text{ m}$ and the system is held at rest. If the system is then released, the maximum speed acquired by each block is
questions.solution:
Let the maximum speed of each block be $v$.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the initial elastic potential energy of the spring is completely converted into the kinetic energy of the two blocks when the spring passes through its natural length.

Initial energy of the system, $E_{i} = \dfrac{1}{2}kx_{0}^{2}$

Final energy of the system, $E_{f} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = mv^{2}$

Equating $E_{i}$ and $E_{f}$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}kx_{0}^{2} = mv^{2}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times (0.1)^{2} = 0.5 \times v^{2}$

$50 \times 0.01 = 0.5 v^{2}$

$0.5 = 0.5 v^{2}$

$v^{2} = 1 \Rightarrow v = 1\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2$ kg, initially at rest at the origin, is subjected to a constant force $\vec{F} = (4\hat{i} + c\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ N. It reaches a position vector $\vec{r} = (2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ m with a speed of $5$ m/s. The value of the unknown component $c$ is:
questions.question: A particle of mass $2$ kg, initially at rest at the origin, is subjected to a constant force $\vec{F} = (4\hat{i} + c\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ N. It reaches a position vector $\vec{r} = (2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ m with a speed of $5$ m/s. The value of the unknown component $c$ is:
questions.solution:
According to the Work-Energy Theorem, the total work done on the particle equals its change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

Given $m = 2$ kg, $v = 5$ m/s, and $u = 0$ m/s:
$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(5)^2 - 0 = 25$ J

The work done by the constant force is also given by the dot product of the force and the displacement vector. Since the particle starts at the origin, the displacement vector is simply the final position vector $\vec{r}$.
$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{r}$
$W = (4\hat{i} + c\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$
$W = (4)(2) + (c)(-3) + (2)(1)$
$W = 8 - 3c + 2$
$W = 10 - 3c$

Equating the two expressions for work done:
$10 - 3c = 25$
$-3c = 15$
$c = -5$

Answer: $-5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $0.5$ kg moves in a circular path of radius $2$ m. Its speed varies with time according to the equation $v = 2t^2$ m/s, where $t$ is in seconds. The total power delivered by the net force acting on the particle at $t = 2$ s is :
questions.question: A particle of mass $0.5$ kg moves in a circular path of radius $2$ m. Its speed varies with time according to the equation $v = 2t^2$ m/s, where $t$ is in seconds. The total power delivered by the net force acting on the particle at $t = 2$ s is :
questions.solution:
The net force on a particle in circular motion has two components: tangential force ($F_t$) and centripetal force ($F_c$).

Since the centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector, it does zero work and delivers zero power. The total power is delivered entirely by the tangential force.

Power $P = \vec{F}_{net} \cdot \vec{v} = F_t v$

Given $v = 2t^2$, the tangential acceleration is:
$a_t = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 4t$

At $t = 2$ s:
$v = 2(2)^2 = 8$ m/s
$a_t = 4(2) = 8$ m/s$^2$

The tangential force is:
$F_t = m a_t = 0.5 \times 8 = 4$ N

The total power delivered at $t = 2$ s is:
$P = F_t v = 4 \times 8 = 32$ W

Answer: $32$ W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block A of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from the top of a smooth curved track of height $5\text{ m}$. At the bottom of the track, it enters a rough horizontal surface and immediately undergoes a perfectly inelastic collision with a stationary block B of mass $3\text{ kg}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the combined mass and the horizontal surface is $0.4$. The distance the combined mass slides before coming to rest is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A small block A of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest from the top of a smooth curved track of height $5\text{ m}$. At the bottom of the track, it enters a rough horizontal surface and immediately undergoes a perfectly inelastic collision with a stationary block B of mass $3\text{ kg}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the combined mass and the horizontal surface is $0.4$. The distance the combined mass slides before coming to rest is (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Velocity of block A at the bottom of the smooth track:
$u = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$

By conservation of linear momentum during the perfectly inelastic collision:
$m_A u = (m_A + m_B) v$
$2 \times 10 = (2 + 3) v \Rightarrow v = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

By the work-energy theorem on the combined mass, the initial kinetic energy is equal to the work done against friction:
$\dfrac{1}{2}(m_A + m_B)v^2 = \mu(m_A + m_B)gd$

Solving for the stopping distance $d$:
$d = \dfrac{v^2}{2\mu g} = \dfrac{4^2}{2 \times 0.4 \times 10}$
$d = \dfrac{16}{8} = 2\text{ m}$

Answer: $2\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of mass $11\text{ kg}$ is pulled along a rough horizontal floor at a constant velocity by a force applied at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. If the work done by this pulling force over a displacement of $10\text{ m}$ is $400\text{ J}$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.question:
A block of mass $11\text{ kg}$ is pulled along a rough horizontal floor at a constant velocity by a force applied at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. If the work done by this pulling force over a displacement of $10\text{ m}$ is $400\text{ J}$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.solution:
Let the pulling force be $F$. The work done by this force is given by:
$W = F d \cos \theta$
$400 = F \times 10 \times \cos 37^{\circ}$
$400 = 10 F \times \dfrac{4}{5} \Rightarrow F = 50\text{ N}$

The normal force $N$ on the block is reduced by the vertical component of the pulling force:
$N = mg - F \sin 37^{\circ}$
$N = 11 \times 10 - 50 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 110 - 30 = 80\text{ N}$

Since the block moves at a constant velocity, the net horizontal force is zero. Thus, the horizontal component of the pulling force equals the kinetic friction:
$F \cos 37^{\circ} = \mu_k N$
$50 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \mu_k \times 80$
$40 = 80 \mu_k \Rightarrow \mu_k = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A particle is given a negligible push from the top of a smooth fixed solid hemisphere of radius $15\text{ m}$. It slides down the surface and eventually loses contact with it. The speed of the particle at the exact moment it loses contact with the hemisphere is:

(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question:
A particle is given a negligible push from the top of a smooth fixed solid hemisphere of radius $15\text{ m}$. It slides down the surface and eventually loses contact with it. The speed of the particle at the exact moment it loses contact with the hemisphere is:

(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the particle lose contact with the hemisphere at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical.

At this position, the forces acting along the radial direction are the component of gravity $mg\cos\theta$ towards the center and the normal reaction $N$ away from the center. The net radial force provides the necessary centripetal acceleration:
$mg\cos\theta - N = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

The condition for the particle to lose contact is $N = 0$. Therefore:
$mg\cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$
$v^2 = gR\cos\theta$

Now, applying conservation of mechanical energy from the top of the hemisphere to this point. The vertical distance fallen by the particle is $h = R - R\cos\theta = R(1 - \cos\theta)$.
Loss in potential energy = Gain in kinetic energy
$mgR(1 - \cos\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Substituting $v^2 = gR\cos\theta$ into the energy equation:
$mgR(1 - \cos\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}m(gR\cos\theta)$
$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos\theta$
$1 = \dfrac{3}{2}\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Now, substitute $\cos\theta$ back to find the speed $v$:
$v^2 = gR\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$
$v^2 = 10 \times 15 \times \dfrac{2}{3}$
$v^2 = 100$
$v = 10\text{ m/s}$

Answer: $10\text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is dropped from a height $H$ onto a horizontal floor. During the collision with the floor, the ball loses $75\%$ of its kinetic energy. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor, and the maximum height it reaches after the first bounce, respectively, are :
questions.question: A ball is dropped from a height $H$ onto a horizontal floor. During the collision with the floor, the ball loses $75\%$ of its kinetic energy. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor, and the maximum height it reaches after the first bounce, respectively, are :
questions.solution:
Let the initial kinetic energy just before the collision be $K_i = mgH$.

Since the ball loses $75\%$ of its kinetic energy during the collision, the kinetic energy retained just after the collision is $K_f = 25\%$ of $K_i = 0.25 mgH$.

The maximum height $h$ reached after the bounce is determined by the retained kinetic energy:
$mgh = K_f = 0.25 mgH \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{H}{4}$

The coefficient of restitution $e$ is the ratio of the speed of separation to the speed of approach:
$e = \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_f}{K_i}} = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$

Thus, the coefficient of restitution is $0.5$ and the rebound height is $\dfrac{H}{4}$.

Answer: $0.5, \dfrac{H}{4}$

questions.q:
A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is pushed up a rough inclined plane of angle $45^{\circ}$ at a constant velocity by a strictly horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $0.5$. The work done by the horizontal applied force as the block moves a distance of $5\text{ m}$ up the incline is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question:
A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is pushed up a rough inclined plane of angle $45^{\circ}$ at a constant velocity by a strictly horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $0.5$. The work done by the horizontal applied force as the block moves a distance of $5\text{ m}$ up the incline is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the horizontal applied force be $F$. We resolve the forces parallel and perpendicular to the inclined plane.
The normal force $N$ is given by the component of weight and the component of the horizontal force pushing into the incline:
$N = mg \cos 45^{\circ} + F \sin 45^{\circ}$

Since the block moves up the incline at a constant velocity, the net force along the incline is zero. The component of $F$ up the incline balances the component of weight and the kinetic friction down the incline:
$F \cos 45^{\circ} = mg \sin 45^{\circ} + \mu_k N$
$F \cos 45^{\circ} = mg \sin 45^{\circ} + \mu_k (mg \cos 45^{\circ} + F \sin 45^{\circ})$

Substituting $m = 2\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\mu_k = 0.5$, and $\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:
$\dfrac{F}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{2}} + 0.5 \left( \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{F}{\sqrt{2}} \right)$

Multiplying the entire equation by $\sqrt{2}$:
$F = 20 + 0.5(20 + F)$
$F = 20 + 10 + 0.5 F$
$0.5 F = 30 \Rightarrow F = 60\text{ N}$

The work done by the horizontal force over a displacement $d = 5\text{ m}$ up the incline is:
$W = F d \cos 45^{\circ}$
$W = 60 \times 5 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{300}{\sqrt{2}} = 150\sqrt{2}\text{ J}$

Answer: $150\sqrt{2}\text{ J}$

questions.q: A block of mass $2\ \text{kg}$, initially at rest, is pulled by a force such that the power delivered by the net force is constant at $9\ \text{W}$. The net work done on the block by the time it has moved a distance of $16\ \text{m}$ is
questions.question: A block of mass $2\ \text{kg}$, initially at rest, is pulled by a force such that the power delivered by the net force is constant at $9\ \text{W}$. The net work done on the block by the time it has moved a distance of $16\ \text{m}$ is
questions.solution:
The power delivered by the net force is given as constant $P = 9\ \text{W}$.

We know that power $P = Fv = m a v = m v \dfrac{dv}{dt}$.
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$, so we can write:
$P = m v^2 \dfrac{dv}{dx}$

Separating the variables and integrating from $x = 0$ to $x = 16\ \text{m}$ and $v = 0$ to $v = v_f$:
$\int_0^{v_f} m v^2 dv = \int_0^x P dx$

$\dfrac{m v_f^3}{3} = P x$

Substitute the given values ($m = 2\ \text{kg}$, $P = 9\ \text{W}$, $x = 16\ \text{m}$):
$\dfrac{2 v_f^3}{3} = 9 \times 16$
$\dfrac{2 v_f^3}{3} = 144$
$v_f^3 = \dfrac{144 \times 3}{2} = 216$

Taking the cube root, we get the final velocity:
$v_f = 6\ \text{m/s}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - 0$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(6)^2 = 36\ \text{J}$

Answer: $36\ \text{J}$

The surface roughness varies such that the coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the position $x$ as $\mu(x) = 0.03 x^2$, where $x$ is in meters. The work done against friction as the block moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 10\text{ m}$ is: (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question: A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ is pulled along a horizontal surface. The surface roughness varies such that the coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the position $x$ as $\mu(x) = 0.03 x^2$, where $x$ is in meters. The work done against friction as the block moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 10\text{ m}$ is: (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Given:
Mass of the block, $m = 5\text{ kg}$
Coefficient of friction, $\mu(x) = 0.03 x^2$
Initial position, $x_1 = 0$
Final position, $x_2 = 10\text{ m}$

The frictional force is variable and depends on position:
$f(x) = \mu(x) m g = (0.03 x^2)(5)(10) = 1.5 x^2\text{ N}$

The work done against friction is the integral of the frictional force over the displacement:
$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(x) \, dx$
$W = \int_{0}^{10} 1.5 x^2 \, dx$
$W = 1.5 \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{10}$
$W = 0.5 \times (10^3 - 0^3) = 0.5 \times 1000 = 500\text{ J}$

Answer: $500\text{ J}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $2$ kg moves along a straight line starting from rest. The power delivered to it by the net force is given by $P = 4t^3$ W, where $t$ is the time in seconds. The magnitude of the net force acting on the particle as a function of time is :
questions.question: A particle of mass $2$ kg moves along a straight line starting from rest. The power delivered to it by the net force is given by $P = 4t^3$ W, where $t$ is the time in seconds. The magnitude of the net force acting on the particle as a function of time is :
questions.solution:
Power $P = F v = m a v = m v \dfrac{dv}{dt}$

Given $m = 2$ kg and $P = 4t^3$ W, we have:
$2 v \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 4t^3$
$v dv = 2t^3 dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ (where $v = 0$) to $t$:
$\int_0^v v' dv' = \int_0^t 2t'^3 dt'$
$\dfrac{v^2}{2} = \dfrac{2t^4}{4}$
$v^2 = t^4 \Rightarrow v = t^2$

The acceleration of the particle is:
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 2t$

The magnitude of the net force is:
$F = ma = 2(2t) = 4t$ N

Answer: $4t$ N
